AST elevated

ALT (Alanine Aminotransferase) and AST (Aspartate Aminotransferase) are enzymes released from damaged liver cells: 
• ALT: More liver-specific; elevated primarily with hepatocellular damage (hepatitis, fatty liver, drug toxicity) 
• AST: Also found in muscle, heart, kidney — less liver-specific 
• ALT > AST: Suggests NAFLD/viral hepatitis 
• AST:ALT ratio >2:1: Suggests alcoholic liver disease 
• Mild elevation (1-3x normal): Often fatty liver, medication effects 
• Marked elevation (>10x normal): Acute hepatitis, drug-induced liver injury, ischemic hepatitis 
Elevated liver enzymes should always be further investigated with a full liver function panel, hepatitis serology, ultrasound, and FIB-4 score.

1. **Limit/avoid alcohol** — No safe amount if you have liver disease 
2. **Maintain healthy weight** — Obesity is a major risk for NAFLD and liver cancer

6. **Never share needles** — Major route of hepatitis C transmission 
7. **Avoid unnecessary medications** — Especially herbal supplements (many are hepatotoxic)

Hepatitis B (HBV) is a viral liver infection transmitted through blood, sexual contact, and mother-to-baby. 296 million people live with chronic HBV worldwide. Most adults (95%) clear acute HBV; 5% develop chronic infection. Chronic HBV can lead to cirrhosis and liver cancer. Diagnosis: HBsAg positive >6 months. end stage liver

Cirrhosis is irreversible scarring (fibrosis) of the liver that disrupts its normal architecture. It is the final stage of chronic liver disease. Causes: Alcohol, NAFLD/NASH, hepatitis B/C, autoimmune hepatitis, and more. Complications include ascites, variceal bleeding, hepatic encephalopathy, hepatorenal syndrome, and hepatocellular carcinoma. Compensated cirrhosis (no major complications) has a good prognosis (>10 year median survival). Decompensated cirrhosis (with complications) has poor prognosis (~6 months without transplant if MELD ≥21). Treatment focuses on treating the cause, managing complications, and liver transplant for end-stage disease.

hepatitis A vaccine

Hepatitis A (HAV) is a self-limiting viral liver infection transmitted via the fecal-oral route (contaminated food/water). Symptoms: Fever, fatigue, nausea, jaundice, dark urine, pale stools — appear 15-50 days after exposure. Most people recover fully in 2-3 months with supportive care only (no antiviral treatment needed). Rarely causes acute liver failure. Prevention: 2-dose Hepatitis A vaccine is >94% effective. Recommended for all children and travelers to endemic regions. Good hand hygiene and safe food/water are also key.

right upper quadrant pain

Pain or discomfort in the right upper quadrant (RUQ) of the abdomen can indicate liver inflammation (hepatitis), liver enlargement (hepatomegaly), gallbladder disease, or, in advanced disease, liver congestion. Liver pain itself is usually a dull ache or pressure, as the liver has no pain receptors — pain comes from stretching of its outer capsule (Glisson's capsule). A clinical evaluation with LFTs, ultrasound, and physical examination is needed for accurate diagnosis.

Jaundice (yellowing of the skin and eyes) is caused by a buildup of bilirubin in the blood, which often signals liver dysfunction. It becomes clinically visible when total bilirubin exceeds 2 mg/dL. Common causes include hepatitis, cirrhosis, bile duct obstruction, and hemolysis. Associated symptoms include dark urine (tea-colored), pale/clay-colored stools, and pruritus (itching). Please see a doctor promptly — jaundice requires proper diagnosis.

Hepatocellular Carcinoma (HCC) is the most common primary liver cancer, arising mainly from cirrhosis. Risk factors: Cirrhosis (any cause), chronic HBV or HCV infection, alcohol, NAFLD/NASH, aflatoxin. Surveillance: Ultrasound + AFP every 6 months for all cirrhotic patients. Hepatitis C (HCV) is a curable viral liver infection spread mainly through blood-to-blood contact (sharing needles). 58 million people live with chronic HCV worldwide. 70-75% of those acutely infected develop chronic HCV; most have no symptoms for decades. Chronic HCV leads to cirrhosis and liver cancer if untreated. Modern treatment: Direct-acting antivirals (DAAs) cure >95% of patients in 8-12 weeks. No vaccine exists; prevention requires avoiding needle sharing.

Cirrhosis is irreversible scarring (fibrosis) of the liver that disrupts its normal architecture. It is the final stage of chronic liver disease. Treatment focuses on treating the cause, managing complications, and liver transplant for end-stage disease.
